section.title: Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem

introduction.p: Rolle’s Theorem combines the existence of absolute extrema with the zero-derivative condition at an interior extremum. The Mean Value Theorem extends the result to unequal endpoint values.
For example, a car moving from mile marker 10 at noon to mile marker 160 at 3{:}00 has average velocity

The car’s velocity may vary during the trip. The Mean Value Theorem guarantees an instant when it equals the average velocity.

exercise.title: Why must some instantaneous rate equal the average rate?

statement.p: The Mean Value Theorem says that, under the right hypotheses, some tangent slope equals the secant slope. In your own words, why is that a statement about motion as well as about graphs, and what would it mean for a speedometer during a trip whose average velocity is known?

hint.p: Average velocity is a net change divided by elapsed time. The theorem claims that this average is actually attained at some instant, provided the trip is continuous and differentiable.

exercise.title: Why do the hypotheses of Rolle’s Theorem and the Mean Value Theorem matter?

statement.p: Explain the roles of continuity on the closed interval, differentiability on its interior, and equal endpoint values in Rolle's Theorem. Which hypotheses fail for a jump or a corner?

hint.p: A jump can skip the needed height, a corner can turn without a horizontal tangent, and a steadily rising graph has no reason to flatten if it starts and ends at different heights.

subsection.title: Consequences of the Mean Value Theorem
subsection.p: The Mean Value Theorem turns information about derivatives into information about functions. That is why it is so useful.

exercise.title: Why does a zero derivative on an interval force a constant function?

statement.p: If f'(x)=0 everywhere on an interval, then f is constant there. In your own words, why does the Mean Value Theorem turn that local information into a global conclusion, and why do two functions with the same derivative differ only by a constant?

hint.p: Between any two inputs, some instantaneous rate equals the average rate. If every instantaneous rate is zero, the net change between those inputs must be zero.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: The Mean Value Theorem explains why the sign of f' controls increasing and decreasing behavior. It also explains why a zero derivative on an interval forces a function to be constant.
But there is more shape left to read.

Two graphs can both be increasing and still look very different. One can rise faster and faster. Another can rise more and more slowly. The first derivative tells us whether the graph rises or falls. The next question asks whether the first derivative itself is increasing or decreasing.
That is the second derivative.
